extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in representative/parliamentary government and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the normative criteria and functional requirements the author identifies as necessary for an effective House of Commons (how Parliament should function, what structural features it needs, and what reforms threaten or preserve its capacities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching function of Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: A great and open council ... ought to teach the nation what it does not know. (Parliament should alter society for the better by educating the public.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate in the House brings unfamiliar notions or grievances into national consciousness; a 'great debate' makes an opinion seem possible and worthy of reckoning even if many disagree. This educational effect is a key public-good function of the Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing function (lay grievances before the nation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament lays grievances and complaints before the nation as the modern counterpart to informing the sovereign; publication of debates makes Parliament inform the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publication of debates means Parliament reports to the nation what is wrong; this counters the tendency of newspapers to repeat only favorable arguments and helps the public hear sides they otherwise would not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative function (law-making as a core role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament's function of legislation is important but not necessarily as important as executive management or political education; legislation is the making of general commands applicable to many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation matters greatly (annual statute-books contain important laws), but much statute-book activity is 'special acts' (single-case enactments) rather than general jurisprudential law. The relative importance of legislation varies with national need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between general laws and special acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A law is a general command applicable to many cases; many statutes are 'special acts' applicable to one case only (e.g., enact that such a railway shall be made from this place to that place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate legislation by whether it lays down general rules or merely resolves single, special transactions; overabundance of special acts can weary committees and suggests a different legislative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial function is not separate in principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly, the House of Commons has no special function with regard to financial matters different from other legislation; financial questions are legislative questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although financial matters recur yearly and have procedural particularities, they are conceptually the same function as other legislation and should be judged on the same grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministerial monopoly on proposing taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: On money the Minister only can propose to tax the people; any member may propose on common subjects but not on money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule concentrates fiscal initiative in the executive and shapes checks and responsibilities: only ministers introduce taxation proposals, which constrains spending proposals from backbenchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet responsibility for national finance as a spending check
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Ministry must 'find the money' for any sanctioned expenditure, the Cabinet has the strongest motive to oppose extra outlay and thus serves as a check on Parliamentary spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executive's financial accountability (it must propose taxes or loans) prevents the 'people's house' from outrunning the people's money; assess fiscal initiatives by whether they respect the Cabinet's responsibility to fund them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament must be an organised body to govern
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons can do work which quarter-sessions or clubs cannot do, because it is an organised body, while quarter-sessions and clubs are unorganised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness depends on institutional organization (procedures, leadership, party structures); large unorganised meetings tend to produce indecision ('a big meeting never does anything').

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership and obedience necessary for parliamentary efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of Parliament obey certain leaders; what those leaders propose they support, what those leaders reject they reject. Without such obedience there would be paralysis (657 amendments to every motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess Parliamentary effectiveness by the presence of recognized leaders who can form and hold a coherent majority; lack of discipline leads to impotence rather than mere inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party is inherent and essential to representative assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment we conceive the House as an elective assembly we perceive that party is of its essence—'There never was an election without a party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize party organization as structural necessity, not a mere optional factionalism. Evaluate reforms or criticisms in light of how they affect party formation and functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat of dissolution as a coercive party discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders can coerce by a threat far more potent than allurement—they can dissolve (Parliament). This threat keeps parties together and enforces majority cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The constitutional power to dissolve Parliament provides an external enforcement mechanism that aligns members with party leadership; the stability of parties should be judged by how such mechanisms affect behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of rank-and-file members is a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The organisation is permanently efficient because it is not composed of warm partisans—'The body is eager, but the atoms are cool.' Members are typically moderate and practical rather than dogmatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A parliament of moderate, pragmatic members is less likely to enact extreme or sectarian policies; evaluate composition by members' tendency toward moderation and practical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders' contact with administrative reality tempers ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders who move from opposition into government confront permanent officials and facts which induce moderation and middle courses; contact with the office tempers party promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership experience in administration is a corrective on ideological excesses. Assess proposed leaders by their familiarity with 'patent facts' and administrative constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituency-driven government undermines parliamentary government
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituency government is the precise opposite of Parliamentary government: it produces immoderate persons far from the scene of action, elicited and sometimes manufactured by local agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the influence of constituencies by whether they produce representatives bound to narrow local passions or to durable, moderate national judgment; excessive constituency control risks paralysis and immoderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Parliament must be composed mainly of moderate men
rubrics_metrics.description: If the overwhelming majority of representatives are not moderate, Parliamentary government will not be possible—immoderate members will elect an immoderate Ministry and enact violent laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess electoral and institutional arrangements by their likelihood to produce a moderate majority; reforms that increase extremes undermine governability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of ultra-democratic equal-vote redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: An ultra-democratic scheme giving each adult an equal vote across uniform districts would create constituencies returning extreme or corrupt representatives (e.g., unmixed squirearchy or representatives of 'public-houses').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how districting and equalization prescriptions affect social composition of representatives: uniform numeric districts can magnify local power structures and produce polarised representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs of voluntary constituencies (Mr. Hare's scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary constituencies allow minorities to combine and reduce wasted votes (merits), but they also make 'constituency-making' a trade and empower organised managers who can manipulate membership and impose party discipline (demerits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the inclusiveness benefits (minority representation, flexible sizing) against the organisational dangers (registration managers, 'member-makers', loss of independence). The voluntary principle risks producing tighter party control than current law-created constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituency-making creates intermediaries (member-makers) who centralize control
rubrics_metrics.description: Under voluntary systems constituency creation would be organised by managers (e.g., Registration Association); these 'member-makers' would select candidates and enforce a rigid party card, producing subservient members bound to committee interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reforms by whether they decentralize or centralize control over candidate selection; intermediary control tends to bind members to party machines and reduce independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caucus effects and systematic manipulation replicate elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: The American presidential selection shows citizens vote for tickets made by caucuses; voluntary constituency-making would produce even worse caucus-like manipulation because the nation cannot reliably choose 658 known great men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative institutional evidence (e.g., caucus systems) to predict distortions: organizational caucuses tend to substitute committee choices for genuine popular selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electioneering corruption risk in local centers (public-houses)
rubrics_metrics.description: In big towns electioneering often centres on 'public-houses' which are centres of illicit corruption and illicit management, producing unprincipled members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the institutional safeguards against local electoral corruption; where corrupt local machines thrive, representative quality suffers.
